transcript.text: How do you decide what to test, when there is never time to test everything?

I'd prioritise the critical paths, the things users actually do most. Unit tests for the business logic and integration tests for the main flows. I mean, try to cover edge cases where things could break. Probably not worth testing simple getters and setters.
Two requests arrive at the same time and both try to update the same record. What can go wrong, and what would you do about it?

You could get a race condition where one update overwrites the other. I'd use a transaction so they don't interfere, or add a lock on the row so the second one has to wait. so, optimistic locking with a version number would also work.
Explain something technical you have worked on to someone who is smart but not an engineer.

I'd use an analogy. Like if I was explaining an API I'd say it's like a waiter in a restaurant, you tell them what you want and they go to the kitchen and bring it back, you don't need to know how the kitchen works. I mean, try to avoid technical terms and check if they're following.
Tell me about a technical decision you made where you were choosing between two reasonable options.

We were deciding between MongoDB and post grass for a project. Mongo was more flexible with the schema which seemed good early on since requirements kept changing, but Postgres had better support for the relational queries we needed. We went with Postgres and it worked out well.
Tell me about the hardest bug you have had to track down. What made it hard?

There was a bug where data was occasionally coming out wrong and it was hard to reproduce. you know, i added a lot of logging to narrow down where it was happening, and eventually found it was a timezone issue where we were converting dates in two different places. Took a few days to find.
